1.title: Task Decomposition, Iteration and Task Types
1.text: Welcome to Module two: Task Decomposition, Iteration and Task Types. This module covers task decomposition, iteration and task types. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. How to break a complex request into steps and review each one. How to iterate: give precise feedback, keep what works, change one thing at a time. How to adapt your prompt to the task type: analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming. When to start over instead of iterating.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedarbrook's Quarterly Review
1.text: Our running case is Cedarbrook Outfitters. Cedarbrook's Quarterly Review. The operations manager pastes sales, returns and complaint data and asks: "Write the quarterly review.". Claude produces a long, shallow document that mixes facts and guesses. The manager restarts with steps: clean the data, find trends, explain causes, draft the review, then check it.

1.title: Task Decomposition
1.text: Task Decomposition. A complex request hides several jobs. Decomposition splits it so each step has a clear input, task and check.

1.title: Task Decomposition, continued
1.text: Task Decomposition, continued. The figure shows this: Task decomposition: clarify the goal, gather the inputs, analyze, draft, then check, with a review point between steps.

1.title: Task Decomposition, continued
1.text: Task Decomposition, continued. one. Clarify. What you ask Claude: "Restate the goal and list what you still need from me". What you check: Goal and scope are right. two. Plan. What you ask Claude: "Propose an outline or approach before writing anything". What you check: The plan fits your need. three. Do the parts. What you ask Claude: One section, one analysis or one question at a time. What you check: Each part against the source data. four. Combine. What you ask Claude: "Assemble the parts into one document in this structure". What you check: Consistency between parts. five. Review. What you ask Claude: "Check the draft against these criteria and list gaps". What you check: Final check by you.

1.title: Task Decomposition, continued
1.text: Task Decomposition, continued. Self-review chain: draft, then review against criteria, then refine is the most common pattern. Ask Claude to critique its own draft against a checklist, then fix it. Decomposition gives you review points: errors are caught early and cheaply instead of being buried in a long answer. You can do the whole chain in one conversation, one step per message, or ask for the plan first and approve it. Very hard reasoning inside one step (math, tricky logic) may benefit from extended thinking (Module six). Exam tip: For a long, multi-part business deliverable, the best first move is to ask for a plan or split the work into reviewed steps, not to send one huge request and hope.

1.title: Iteration
1.text: Iteration. Your first prompt is a draft of a request. Treat the first answer as a starting point and refine.

1.title: Iteration, continued
1.text: Iteration, continued. Say exactly what to change: "shorter intro, add the return rate, friendlier tone". Say "make it better". Keep what works: "keep sections one and three as they are". Re-ask everything and lose good parts. Change one or two things at a time so you see what helped. Rewrite the whole prompt each time. Give examples of what you want. Describe a style abstractly only. Add the missing context the first answer revealed. Repeat the same prompt expecting a different result. Ask Claude to explain its choices or list assumptions. Accept unexplained decisions.

1.title: Iteration, continued
1.text: Iteration, continued. Compare versions: ask for two variants (for example, a formal and a casual one) and choose, or merge the best parts. Edit an earlier message to branch the conversation: the original thread stays, and you get a separate version to compare. Start a new chat when the thread has drifted, gotten very long, or contains wrong assumptions (Module eight). Paste a short summary of what you decided. Stop iterating when the output meets the criteria you set at the start. More rounds add cost without value.

1.title: Iteration, continued
1.text: Iteration, continued. The figure shows this: The iteration loop: prompt, review, give specific feedback, revise, and stop when the criteria are met. Exam tip: Good iteration feedback is specific, actionable and tied to your criteria. "Cut to one hundred words and add the price" beats "improve it".

1.title: Adapt the Prompt to the Task Type
1.text: Adapt the Prompt to the Task Type. Analysis. Goal: Find patterns, compare, explain. Prompt strategy: Provide the data, define the question and the output; ask for assumptions and the figures used; ask it to show steps. Feature that helps: Upload files; thinking for hard reasoning; check numbers yourself. Research. Goal: Gather and synthesize information. Prompt strategy: State the question, scope and time frame; ask for sources; ask for disagreements among sources; verify key claims. Feature that helps: Web search for quick facts; Research for deep, multi-source reports.

1.title: Adapt the Prompt to the Task Type, continued
1.text: Adapt the Prompt to the Task Type, continued. Drafting. Goal: Produce text for a reader. Prompt strategy: Give audience, purpose, tone, length, key facts; ask for a draft; then iterate on edits. Feature that helps: Projects hold voice guides; styles. Brainstorming. Goal: Generate options. Prompt strategy: Ask for many options (ten to twenty); encourage variety; set criteria to pick later; then ask to develop the best two or three. Feature that helps: Chat; ask for a table scoring options. Analysis: ask "what assumptions did you make?" and "show the calculation". Claude can slip on arithmetic, so verify critical numbers (Module four).

1.title: Adapt the Prompt to the Task Type, continued
1.text: Adapt the Prompt to the Task Type, continued. Research: separate finding from concluding. Ask for sources, then check the originals. For a current fact (a price, a rule), use web search; for a comprehensive report, use Research. Drafting: the first draft is for editing. Specify the voice; ask for an alternative opening; keep your final edit. Brainstorming: quantity first, judgment second. Do not judge too early; later ask Claude to rank by your criteria. Here Claude's imagination is an asset, and errors matter less than in factual tasks. Exam tip: Match the strategy to the task. Factual and analytic tasks need sources, checks and assumptions. Creative tasks need volume and variety. Using a creative approach for a factual task is the trap.

1.title: Putting It Together
1.text: Putting It Together. Plan the brief. Task type: Decomposition. Feature: Chat. Gather rival prices. Task type: Research. Feature: Research (with web search). Compare to our prices. Task type: Analysis. Feature: File upload. Positioning ideas. Task type: Brainstorming. Feature: Chat. Write the brief. Task type: Drafting. Feature: Chat, then edit.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Decompose: Clarify, plan, do the parts, combine, review. Self-review chain: Draft, review against criteria, refine. Feedback: Specific, actionable, tied to criteria; keep what works. Branch: Edit an earlier message to compare versions. Restart: Drifted or very long thread: new chat plus a summary. Analysis: Data plus question; list assumptions; verify numbers. Research: Scope, sources, cross-check; web search (light) or Research (deep). Drafting: Audience, tone, key facts; first draft is for editing. Brainstorming: Quantity and variety first; judge later with criteria.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A manager wants a full competitor analysis, a pricing proposal and a slide outline in one go. What is the best approach? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Decomposing into reviewed steps catches errors early and improves each part.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. After a first draft, a director says "make it better" and gets a similar draft. What should they do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Specific, actionable feedback gives Claude a direction to improve.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Which prompt strategy fits a brainstorming task best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Quantity and variety come first; evaluation comes after.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A team member asks Claude to analyze a sales C S V. Which addition most improves reliability? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Listing assumptions and showing the figures used makes the analysis checkable, which is the best protection against a quiet error.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A conversation has drifted, contains a wrong assumption from an hour ago, and answers are getting worse. What is a sensible response? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A fresh chat with a summary removes the stale assumption (Module eight).

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Select two. Which two describe good decomposition of a long report? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and B. Planning and per-part checks are the point of decomposition.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. For which task is a creative, high-volume approach L E A S T appropriate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Factual and legal summaries need accuracy, sources and review, not volume of variety.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. Why ask Claude to review its draft against criteria before you read it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Self-review is a useful first pass, not a replacement for your own check.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. A strategist needs a current fact: a rival's published price for one product. Which option fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A simple current fact is a light web-search task; Research is for comprehensive reports.

1.title: Practice Question 10
1.text: Question ten. What is the best sign that it is time to stop iterating? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Criteria defined up front tell you when the output is good enough.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all ten answers. Question one: C. Question two: C. Question three: A. Question four: C. Question five: D. Question six: A and B. Question seven: D. Question eight: A. Question nine: C. Question ten: C. In the next module, we continue the course.
